body_en:
Today I came across a video all of three seconds long.

In it, a Chinese middle-school girl sits in the back seat of a car, eating breakfast. It's 5:30 in the morning. She seems used to this life by now — sitting in the car, staring out the window at a sky that hasn't yet broken into dawn, her eyes hollow, chewing mechanically, no spark in her at all. The exhaustion and the numbness reach right through the screen and hit you in the soul.

Her father is driving. Her mother made the breakfast, drove her, and filmed this.

Three short seconds — and behind them, a life one Chinese family repeats every single day.

I don't know what time this girl goes to bed each night. I don't know how her grades are. I don't know how much her parents have given up for her education. But I can almost picture the whole system of life that sits behind this scene.

The child has to get up early, go to class, take exams, and finish mountains of homework. The parents have to get up early, make breakfast, drive her to school, worry about her studies — and still carry their own jobs and lives.

A family like a precisely running machine, everyone working nonstop in their own position.

Everyone is working so hard.

But suddenly I want to ask: what kind of future are they actually running toward?

1. Why a Family's Effort Became a Family's Exhaustion

In China, education was never just one child's business.

More often than not, it's a whole-family project.

From kindergarten on, parents have to think about schools, grades, after-school classes, and every kind of educational resource. By elementary and middle school, the competition heats up: the child's time is filled with classes, homework, exams, and rankings, and the parents slip into a state of long-term tension along with them.

The child competes at school; the parents back her up at home.

To let the child sleep ten more minutes, the parents may have to prepare everything in advance. To save time on the way to school, breakfast moves to the back seat of the car. To avoid falling behind anyone else, the whole family has to pack its life tighter and tighter.

The hardest thing about this life is that nobody has to force it on anyone.

The parents believe it's for the child's own good, and the child knows how much her parents have sacrificed. Everyone is doing their best to play their part.

The parents don't dare let up. The child doesn't dare slack off.

Because both are afraid: stop for a moment, and someone else will overtake you.

But here's a question worth thinking about: when a family has to give up this much rest, time, and quality of life just to hold a child's place in the education race, what has this system actually given the family?

There's a saying we hear all the time: endure the bitterest hardship and you'll rise above the rest.

But the question is: children today endure so much hardship — will they really become who they want to be?

2. The Future We Were Promised Is Slipping Further Away

People used to hold a fairly simple belief about education:

Study hard, get into a good university, find a respectable job, then buy a home, get married, start a family, and live better than your parents did.

That logic once gave countless ordinary families hope.

For people with no connections and no resources, education was at least seen as a relatively fair way up.

But today, that road is getting more crowded by the day.

There are more university graduates than ever, degrees keep losing value, and the job market grows more cutthroat. Even if you finish university without a hitch, there's no guarantee of an ideal job — let alone being able to afford housing, healthcare, retirement, and starting a family.

Things that were once seen as markers of success are becoming unreachable for more and more young people.

Of course, education still matters. Knowledge still has value. And hard work is far from meaningless.

But we have to admit one reality: there has never been a reliable equation between personal effort and final reward.

A child can start working at 5:30 in the morning, study like that for a decade or more, and still face a job market that isn't forgiving.

That doesn't mean she's not good enough. It doesn't mean she didn't work hard enough.

It's just that exam scores were never the only thing deciding a person's future.

Family resources, the social environment, the economic cycle, the structure of the job market, and the era you happen to live in — all of these shape a life.

If we insist on blaming every problem on not working hard enough, then the problems that hard work can't solve end up becoming the individual's burden.

That's not fair to the child. And it's not fair to the parents either.

3. The Scariest Part Isn't the Hardship — It's Treating Hardship as Normal

I'm not against hardship.

In fact, anyone who wants real ability will inevitably have to put in time and effort.

Learning takes focus. Growing up takes grinding. Plenty of worthwhile things are hard by nature.

But what I can't stand is an idea of education that treats suffering itself as valuable.

As if getting up earlier means working harder, sleeping less means being better, doing more means having more hope.

We seem to have grown used to measuring a person's drive by how much they sacrifice.

A child who sleeps until she wakes up naturally might be called lazy. A weekend spent playing might be called a lack of discipline. Refusing extra tutoring might be called wasting your own future.

And so rest became something you have to justify, fun became something you have to atone for, and even the childhood an ordinary kid deserves had to make way for a so-called future.

But I've always believed a person's growth shouldn't be measured by exams alone.

A middle-schooler should have time to exercise, time to read books she actually likes, time to talk with friends, time to be curious about the world — and the right to do nothing at all on some ordinary afternoon.

None of that stands in the way of success.

It's just part of life.

If a child grows up with nothing but exams, rankings, and admissions — never a real chance to feel life itself — then even if she eventually gets into a good university, how should we judge that childhood?

Did we raise a person with independent thoughts, the ability to live, and the capacity to feel happiness? Or a person who's good at completing tasks, following instructions, and chasing the next goal?

4. The Parents Are Trapped in This Race Too

There's another person in that video who's easy to overlook: the parents driving the car.

It's easy to blame the parents, to say they loaded their child with too heavy a life.

But I don't think it's that simple.

Most parents don't have many choices either.

They may be ordinary salaried workers, without substantial family wealth or social resources. What they can give their child is limited, so they give everything they possibly can.

They believe in education. They believe in hard work. They believe that if their child does better than they did, she'll have a chance at a better life.

So they get up early, drive her, make breakfast, worry about her grades, and pay for her education.

They're probably exhausted too — they just never get the chance to stop.

What's sadder still is that this sacrifice usually comes with a quiet anxiety: if I don't do this, will my child lose to someone else?

And so parents and child are strapped onto the same conveyor belt, speeding up all the time.

The parents are afraid the child will fall behind. The child is afraid of letting her parents down.

Everyone is working hard for the other person — but hardly anyone ever stops to ask themselves:

Is this the life we actually want?

5. What Kind of Person Are We Trying to Raise?

I don't want to simply dismiss Chinese education, and I don't think all this effort is for nothing.

Education remains one of the most important ways for ordinary people to gain knowledge, broaden their horizons, and change their circumstances.

But the meaning of education should never be just winning a competition that lasts a decade or more.

It should give a person the ability to think for themselves, the freedom to choose their own life, and the courage to face an unknown world.

A person gets an education not just to find a job someday, pay off a mortgage, carry family responsibilities, and pass the same anxiety on to the next generation.

They should be able to know what they love, what they're willing to work hard for, to appreciate the world, and to decide what kind of life they want to live.

I don't know what university that girl eating breakfast in the back seat at 5:30 in the morning will get into, what job she'll do, or what city she'll live in.

I don't know whether she actually wants to live this way right now.

But I hope her future is more than just payback for all these sacrifices.

I hope that one day she'll truly have the right to choose — instead of moving from one race to the next.

Because the end point of education shouldn't be a life spent forever competing.

5:30 in the morning. The sky hasn't fully brightened yet.

A child sits in the back seat eating breakfast while her parents drive her to school.

To them, this is probably just another ordinary morning.

But what I see is a family's entire hope for the future — and the anxiety that countless ordinary families in this era are carrying together.

I don't want to mock their hard work, and I certainly don't want to deny a parent's love for their child.

I just can't help asking:

If a child has to start burning through her childhood before the sky is even light; if a pair of parents has to pour most of their lives into a race with no guaranteed outcome — are we really working toward a better life, or have we forgotten what life is supposed to look like?

We always say: don't let your child lose at the starting line.

But has anyone seriously asked:

Does life really need a starting line like this?

And when you run to the end of it — what was it all for?
excerpt_en: A three-second clip of a middle-school girl eating breakfast in the back of a car at 5:30 in the morning — and behind it, a whole family running like a machine, and a generation caught in the same race.
title_en: The Child at 5:30 AM: When Hard Work No Longer Promises a Better Future
